solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Almost luxurious benefit

indicators.note: almost means the word falls just short, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A perk that is nearly lavish, but not quite.
explanation.definitionFit: A plus is an advantage or added bonus, so it works as a noun synonym for benefit.

clue.text: Person selling soul shortly receives brief time as a celebrity

indicators.note: receives means the shortened name takes another piece inside it
shortly means the name is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: Faust is the legendary scholar who sold his soul to the Devil
a mo is a moment, a brief time

explanation.surface: Someone who sold out briefly gets a taste of stardom.
explanation.walkthrough: Faust is the scholar of legend who traded his soul to the Devil; 'shortly' drops his last letter before 'receives' takes in the brief time.
explanation.definitionFit: Being well known to the public is what it means to be a celebrity, so 'as a celebrity' describes someone renowned.

clue.text: Perhaps pasty, the man is in an underground club

indicators.note: in means one piece is placed within the club word

parts.note: a dive is a seedy, often basement, club or bar
the man is, contracted, gives he's

explanation.surface: A man who is pale, perhaps, in a basement nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pasty' looks like a pale complexion or a pie, but here it means paste-like, i.e. sticky.
explanation.definitionFit: Paste is used as glue, so something pasty is, perhaps, sticky; 'Perhaps' marks the example.

clue.text: Roast lamb is often rolling in it

definitions.meaning: roast lamb is traditionally served with mint sauce, i.e. flavoured with mint
rolling in it means very rich

explanation.definitionFit: British slang for wealthy, and also the past participle of flavouring with mint, as roast lamb usually is.

clue.text: Terrible route to mention when climbing

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means the word is read upwards, i.e. backwards

explanation.surface: A mountaineer complains about a dreadful route to bring up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when climbing' turns CITE into ETIC, read up the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathetic is used colloquially to mean miserably poor or inadequate, a synonym of terrible.

clue.text: Something in head of Chancellor, non-conformist Liberal with indecisive comment

parts.note: CE stands for Chancellor of the Exchequer

explanation.surface: A dissenting Liberal hesitates, in the head of a Chancellor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head of Chancellor' tempts you to take a C; 'Something in head' is the definition and 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The part of the brain at the back of the skull controlling balance and movement is literally something in the head.

clue.text: Line with point in middle of square that's parallel to radius

indicators.note: in means the line and point sit within the other letters
middle of takes the central letters of the six-letter word square

parts.note: N is a compass point, north

explanation.surface: Geometry: a line through the middle of a square, parallel to a circle's radius.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is geometry; 'radius' is really the forearm bone.
explanation.definitionFit: The two forearm bones lie side by side, so the one paired with the radius runs parallel to it.

clue.text: Detective having had enough swallows drink to become wasted

indicators.note: swallows means one word takes another into it

explanation.surface: A policeman, already full, keeps drinking until drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to become' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Dissipated describes someone worn out by overindulgence; wasted is a near synonym, also suggesting drunkenness.

clue.text: Eloquent version of golden virtues

indicators.note: a version of something is a reworking, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Eloquence as a variant of golden virtues, since speech is silver and silence golden.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone silver-tongued speaks persuasively and fluently, which is to be eloquent.

clue.text: Drug mule's first in run-of-the-mill turns to get through barrier

indicators.note: turns means the assembled letters are read backwards
in means the initial letter sits inside the ordinary word
first takes only the opening letter of mule's

explanation.surface: A drug mule turns to the ordinary to slip through a border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts M inside SOSO; E goes in front, and 'turns' reads ESOMSO backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Osmosis is diffusion through a membrane, so the verb means to pass through a barrier.

clue.text: Absence irregularly interrupted by those people, which allows access to unsupervised children

indicators.note: irregularly interrupted by means each word breaks into the other at intervals, letters interleaved

explanation.surface: Something that gives access to children left on their own.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words interleave: L A (T) C (H) K (E Y). The clue reads as 'which allows access', but the definition is the latchkey kids.
explanation.definitionFit: Children who let themselves into an empty home after school are known by the key they carry, a name for unsupervised kids.

clue.text: Directions almost diametrically opposed anger in source of stories

parts.note: west-south-west is nearly opposite north-east on the compass

explanation.surface: Points of view almost opposed, with fury feeding the news.
explanation.walkthrough: North-east's true opposite is south-west; WSW is just off it, hence 'almost'.
explanation.definitionFit: A news agency feed supplies reports to newspapers, so it is a source of stories.

clue.text: European lives here now, worried political leader

indicators.note: worried means these letters are troubled into a new order

explanation.surface: An anxious European living here now under some politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' rearranges HERE NOW to ENHOWER.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwight Eisenhower was the 34th US President, a political leader after commanding Allied forces.

clue.text: Inability to choose? Find it here!

indicators.note: the exclamation turns find it here into a pointer at the clue's own last words, where the letters lie

explanation.surface: A puzzle setter's dare: can't decide? Look right here!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Find it here!' does double duty: the exclamation points at the very words the answer runs across, so no separate word acts as indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Vacillating indecision, being unable to make up one's mind, is dithering.

clue.text: Tailor spec to reality, matching conventional ideas

indicators.note: to tailor is to alter or adapt, so these letters are refitted

explanation.surface: Adjust a specification to what is real, fitting accepted notions.
explanation.definitionFit: Stereotypical means conforming to a fixed, oversimplified image, i.e. matching conventional ideas.

clue.text: Young woman hugged by emotional, topless diplomat

indicators.note: hugged by means the girl sits inside the trimmed word
topless in a down clue means the first letter goes

parts.note: a miss is a young woman

explanation.surface: A tearful, half-dressed envoy embraces a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' removes the first letter of the emotional word (top, as this is a down clue), giving EARY, and 'hugged by' wraps that round the young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: An emissary is an envoy sent on a mission, and a diplomat performs that role.

clue.text: Held an attitude about accepting one god

indicators.note: accepting means the first word takes another inside it

parts.note: posed means held a stance or attitude
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone struck a pose about accepting a single deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Poseidon is the Greek god of the sea, so god is a direct category for him.

clue.text: Savoury ingredient the writer's added to dénouement

indicators.note: added to means the second piece follows the first

parts.note: a dénouement is the end of a story
the writer's, i.e. the writer has, gives I've

explanation.surface: An author has tacked a savoury touch onto the plot's ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the writer's' is 'the writer has', shortened to I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: Endive is a bitter salad leaf used in savoury dishes, so an ingredient of that kind.

clue.text: "Towering" engineer to hear and a lot to see

indicators.note: to hear means the engineer's name is said aloud

parts.note: Gustave Eiffel built the Eiffel Tower in Paris

explanation.surface: Seeing and hearing about a towering engineer is plenty to take in.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyeful is a good long look, or a striking sight: a lot to see.

clue.text: Alien craft reversing round satellite circling sun, out of a novel

indicators.note: reversing means the whole assembly is read backwards
circling means the satellite surrounds the next piece
novel means new, so the remaining letters are rearranged
out of means the following letter is removed

explanation.surface: A novel's alien spacecraft reverses around a moon orbiting a sun.
explanation.walkthrough: STAR loses A ('out of a') to STR, 'novel' turns it to RTS, 'circling' puts it in MOON, O goes first, and 'reversing' reads OMORTSON backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The doomed towing spaceship in the 1979 film Alien is named after Conrad's novel.

clue.text: What's right on a plate (for vegetarians)?

definitions.text: What's right on a plate (for vegetarians)?

explanation.surface: Asking what belongs on a vegetarian's dinner plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link: R comes before A DISH.
explanation.definitionFit: A red root vegetable eaten in salads, it suits a vegetarian's plate.

clue.text: French marine explorer about to eject his water

parts.note: eau is French for water, the Frenchman's own word

explanation.surface: A French diver is about to expel water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' looks like a phrase; 'about' gives C and 'his water' is French because he is.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacques Cousteau was the French undersea explorer who co-invented the aqualung.

clue.text: Provoke Mussolini with name for Left

indicators.note: name for Left means one letter replaces the other

explanation.surface: Mussolini named in place of the Left, a provocation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' swaps N in place of L in IL DUCE.
explanation.definitionFit: To induce is to bring about or prompt, so it can mean to provoke a reaction.

clue.text: Clubs mostly tolerate someone brash

parts.note: C is clubs in card games

indicators.note: mostly means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: to have, as in 'I won't have it', is to tolerate

explanation.surface: Clubs mostly put up with a loudmouth.
explanation.walkthrough: A chav is British slang for a flashy, loutish young person.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a loud, flashily dressed, uncouth young person, so someone brash.

clue.text: Eventually do understand wife excluded from second part of bout

parts.note: a round is part of a boxing bout

indicators.note: excluded from means the letter is taken out of the number word

parts.note: second here is the number two

explanation.surface: Get it: a wife is barred from the second round of the fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second part of bout' reads as round two, but 'second' is the number with W removed, and 'part of bout' is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To get round to something is to find time to do it at last, eventually.

clue.text: Lush, small wood

explanation.surface: A small, lush wood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lush' looks like an adjective for verdant woodland, but it is the noun: a drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A soak is a heavy drinker, and lush is slang for the same.
